sections.html:
One department, Tax Administration, does the work many counties split between an assessor and a collector. The staff appraise houses and business equipment, mail the bills, accept payments, review relief and exemption requests, and maintain ownership records, tax maps and GIS layers.

The office is at 357 Ferrell Lane in the town of Halifax (zip 27839). Mail goes to P.O. Box 68. Call 252-583-2121. The counter runs half past eight to five, Monday to Friday, and the county's pay page links to online property tax payment.

Halifax County has about 46,534 residents, 25,078 homes and apartments, and a middle owned-home value of $106,200. Owners occupy 62.9% of occupied homes, and only 75 permits for new building were issued in 2025.

sections.h2: Taxes must be settled before a deed can record
sections.html:
A county rule dated January 1, 2016 tells the Register of Deeds to refuse any deed that moves title to real property until the Tax Collector certifies that the described parcel carries no lien for delinquent property tax or any other tax the collector enforces.

For a seller, that is a gate in front of closing. Staff need time to research the parcel, so the deed has to reach the collector's office between 8:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. Before recording is scheduled, ask your closing attorney to confirm the certification is done.

The county also handles town taxes through a tax agency fund. Request a payoff figure well ahead of closing and ask whether a municipal balance shows on the parcel.

The ordinance for the year beginning July 1, 2026 levies $0.70 on every $100 of property listed as of January 1, 2026. Five cents of that is reserved to repay the installment contract dated May 26, 2016 that financed the school replacing Manning Elementary.

More layers may sit on top, depending on location. The ordinance also covers school supplements, fire districts and town collections for Enfield, Halifax, Hobgood, Littleton, Roanoke Rapids, Scotland Neck and Weldon.

Separate rates apply in eleven fire districts: Arcola, Darlington, Davie, Enfield, Halifax, Hobgood, Littleton, Rheasville, Scotland Neck, Tillery and Weldon. Phone the tax office to learn your district and whether a town rate applies to you.

The bill is payable September 1, and a payment made through January 5 carries no interest. Interest then runs at 2% for the rest of January and at three-fourths of a percent for each month or part month afterward.

Listing happens in January and closes January 31, though commissioners can add 30 days in an ordinary year or 60 in a revaluation year. A prepayment discount exists only when the governing board sets a schedule before the due date, so ask Tax Administration whether Halifax offers one. The postmark governs mailed checks.

The county budget moves $100,000 into a revaluation fund for 2026-27. State law requires reappraisal of real property at least every eight years. The tax office can tell you the year your current values took effect.

Start with the county's equalization board, formally the Board of Equalization and Review. Commissioners fill that role unless a separate board has been created, and the board starts meeting in April or early May. Your request for a hearing must reach it before it adjourns.

In years without a revaluation the board finishes in a few weeks and stops by July 1. In a revaluation year it can work until December 1. A decision follows within a month of adjournment. The next level is the state Property Tax Commission, where a written notice stating your grounds is due thirty days after the board's mailing, with a copy for the assessor.

Boards respond to evidence tied to the revaluation date, such as sales of similar homes, an independent appraisal or repair quotes. Tax Administration can give you that date for Halifax.

sections.h2: Which relief programs can a homeowner claim?
sections.html:
Three state programs exist, and each owner may use just one. Form AV-9 goes to the county assessor. January is the intended window, yet the assessor must accept applications through June 1 before the tax year begins.

  • Elderly or disabled exclusion: excludes $25,000 or 50% of the home's appraised value, whichever is more. The owner is a North Carolina resident who, as of January 1, is at least 65 or totally and permanently disabled and whose income falls below $38,800 for 2026.
  • Circuit breaker: holds the bill to 4% of income, or 5% for income between that limit and $58,200. The owner needs five years of owning and living in the home. Postponed tax stays as a lien and falls due when the home transfers.
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: excludes $45,000 of value, and no age or income test applies. Form NCDVA-9 is completed first with a veteran service officer and then filed with the assessor.

Seniors make up 25.2% of Halifax's population, and 16.3% of people under 65 report a disability, so these programs reach a large share of owners.

Unpaid tax becomes a lien from the January 1 listing date. To collect, the county files a foreclosure suit locally, and notice goes to the record owner, the spouse and other lienholders.

Halifax advertises each scheduled tax foreclosure on its website. The sale rules are:

  • Bidding happens in the courthouse's lower lobby in the town of Halifax.
  • Every bid stays open to upset for 10 days.
  • Property sells as is, and neither the county nor the commissioner warrants title or condition.
  • Bidders should consider a title examination, and skipping one does not release a bid.

Before confirmation, an owner can redeem by paying the tax bill together with penalties, interest and court costs. Any money left after the taxes is held by the court for those entitled to it. Selling beforehand leaves the equity in your hands. Call the county Legal Department at 252-583-3612 about a scheduled sale.

Get a payoff figure from Tax Administration and clear the balance first, which lets the collector certify the parcel. Then give your attorney the vesting deed and payoff letters. Recording follows the certification, and the register will not take the deed without it. A cash sale skips a lender's review, but the tax certification still applies. Recording after a sale is covered in our Halifax County register of deeds guide.

faqs.q: Where do I find Halifax County Tax Administration?
faqs.a: At 357 Ferrell Lane in Halifax, with P.O. Box 68 for mail and 252-583-2121 for calls. One department handles both valuation and collection, and service runs half past eight to five on weekdays.

faqs.q: Which tax rate does Halifax County charge?
faqs.a: The 2026-27 ordinance sets $0.70 per $100 for the county. Two school administrative units add $0.20 or $0.10, and fire districts and towns add rates that vary by parcel location.

faqs.q: Must a seller clear delinquent taxes before a Halifax County closing?
faqs.a: Yes. A county rule in force since January 1, 2016 bars the register from taking a deed until the Tax Collector certifies the parcel has no delinquent tax lien. Pay any balance first so the certification can issue.

faqs.q: Is it possible to challenge a Halifax County assessment?
faqs.a: Yes. Request a hearing from the county's equalization board before it adjourns in spring. If the board's decision disappoints you, the Property Tax Commission accepts an appeal filed thirty days after the mailing at the latest.

faqs.q: What is a Halifax County tax foreclosure sale like?
faqs.a: It is a public auction in the courthouse lobby. Each bid stays open to a higher offer for 10 days, the house sells as is with no title warranty, and the county posts each notice on its website.
